IMMIGRANT WORKER PROTECTION ACT — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jane Doe · Acme Corp.

SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes selected requirements of California's Immigrant Worker Protection Act (Stats. 2017, Ch. 492 (AB 450)), codified at Labor Code § 90.2 and Government Code §§ 7285.1–7285.3, in connection with Acme Corp.'s employment of Jane Doe. It covers the notice an employer must give current employees after a federal immigration agency gives notice that it will inspect Form I-9 or other employment records, and it covers California's restrictions on an employer voluntarily granting a federal immigration enforcement agent access to nonpublic work areas or to employee records during such an enforcement action. It does not address the separate, hiring-stage Form I-9 verification process, the E-Verify program, the federal anti-discrimination provisions of 8 U.S.C. § 1324b, or Labor Code § 1019.2's separate restriction on reverifying an existing employee's work authorization — each addressed, where covered in this library, in a different information sheet.

NOTICE TO EMPLOYEES OF AN I-9 OR EMPLOYMENT-RECORDS INSPECTION
California law requires an employer, except as otherwise required by federal law, to notify each current employee within 72 hours of receiving a federal immigration agency's notice that it will inspect Form I-9 or other employment records. The employer must give this notice by posting it in the language the employer normally uses to communicate employment-related information to employees, and must separately give written notice within 72 hours to the employee's authorized representative, if any. The posted notice must identify the inspecting agency, the date the employer received the inspection notice, the nature of the inspection to the extent known, and must include a copy of the Notice of Inspection itself. Upon an affected employee's reasonable request, the employer must also provide that employee a copy of the Notice of Inspection.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "an employer shall provide a notice to each current employee, by posting in the language the employer normally uses to communicate employment-related information to the employee, of any inspections of I-9 Employment Eligibility Verification forms or other employment records conducted by an immigration agency within 72 hours of receiving notice of the inspection. Written notice shall also be given within 72 hours to the employee’s authorized representative, if any."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 90.2(a)(1) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Labor Code, duty to notify current employees of a records inspection (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=90.2.)
  "The posted notice shall contain the following information: (A) The name of the immigration agency conducting the inspections of I-9 Employment Eligibility Verification forms or other employment records. (B) The date that the employer received notice of the inspection. (C) The nature of the inspection to the extent known. (D) A copy of the Notice of Inspection of I-9 Employment Eligibility Verification forms for the inspection to be conducted."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 90.2(a)(1) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Labor Code, required contents of the posted notice (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=90.2.)
  "An employer, upon reasonable request, shall provide an affected employee a copy of the Notice of Inspection of I-9 Employment Eligibility Verification forms."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 90.2(a)(3) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Labor Code, copy of the Notice of Inspection on request (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=90.2.)
  Known gap: This is California law, used as evidence of the specific pre-inspection notice duty Labor Code § 90.2(a) creates — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim that any particular employer has received, or will receive, a Notice of Inspection. All three citations below are subdivisions of the same statutory section, § 90.2(a): the first quotes paragraph (a)(1)'s core 72-hour notice duty and its posting-language and authorized-representative requirements; the second quotes paragraph (a)(1)'s list of required notice contents, subparagraphs (A) through (D); the third quotes paragraph (a)(3)'s separate duty to furnish an affected employee a copy of the Notice of Inspection on request. This clause does not cover paragraph (a)(2), a duty running to the Labor Commissioner (not the employer) to develop a model posting by July 1, 2018 — a now-historical administrative deadline this clause's drafter judged not to state an ongoing employer obligation worth quoting. This clause also does not cover the separate post-inspection notice duty in § 90.2(b), addressed in a different clause of this information sheet, or the civil penalty for failing to comply with either notice duty, addressed in a separate clause.

NOTICE TO AFFECTED EMPLOYEES OF INSPECTION RESULTS
Separately from the pre-inspection notice, California law requires an employer, except as otherwise required by federal law, to provide each current affected employee — and that employee's authorized representative, if any — a copy of the written immigration agency notice reporting the inspection's results, within 72 hours of the employer's receipt of that notice. Within the same 72 hours, the employer must also give each affected employee, and the employee's authorized representative, written notice of the obligations the inspection results create for the employer and for that employee. This notice must relate to the affected employee only, must be hand-delivered at the workplace if possible, and otherwise sent by mail and, if the employee's email address is known, by email. The notice must describe any deficiencies identified as to that employee, the time period for correcting them, the time and date of any meeting scheduled to correct them, and the employee's right to representation at that meeting. An "affected employee" is defined as an employee the immigration agency's inspection results identify as potentially lacking work authorization, or whose work-authorization documents the inspection identified as deficient.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "an employer shall provide to each current affected employee, and to the employee’s authorized representative, if any, a copy of the written immigration agency notice that provides the results of the inspection of I-9 Employment Eligibility Verification forms or other employment records within 72 hours of its receipt of the notice."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 90.2(b)(1) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Labor Code, duty to provide a copy of the inspection results (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=90.2.)
  "Within 72 hours of its receipt of this notice, the employer shall also provide to each affected employee, and to the affected employee’s authorized representative, if any, written notice of the obligations of the employer and the affected employee arising from the results of the inspection of I-9 Employment Eligibility Verification forms or other employment records."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 90.2(b)(1) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Labor Code, duty to notify the affected employee of resulting obligations (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=90.2.)
  "The notice shall contain the following information: (A) A description of any and all deficiencies or other items identified in the written immigration inspection results notice related to the affected employee. (B) The time period for correcting any potential deficiencies identified by the immigration agency. (C) The time and date of any meeting with the employer to correct any identified deficiencies. (D) Notice that the employee has the right to representation during any meeting scheduled with the employer."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 90.2(b)(1) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Labor Code, required contents of the results notice (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=90.2.)
  "an “affected employee” is an employee identified by the immigration agency inspection results to be an employee who may lack work authorization, or an employee whose work authorization documents have been identified by the immigration agency inspection to have deficiencies."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 90.2(b)(2) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Labor Code, "affected employee" defined (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=90.2.)
  Known gap: This is California law, used as evidence of the post-inspection notice duty Labor Code § 90.2(b) creates once an employer receives the immigration agency's written results of an I-9 or other employment-records inspection — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim that any particular employee is or will become an "affected employee" as the statute defines that term. All four citations below are subdivisions of the same statutory section: the first three quote paragraph (b)(1) (the results-notice duty, the separate obligations-notice duty, and the required contents of that notice, respectively); the fourth quotes paragraph (b)(2)'s definition of "affected employee." This clause does not independently evaluate whether any particular immigration-agency communication would qualify as the "written immigration agency notice" the statute describes, and does not cover the pre-inspection notice duty of § 90.2(a), addressed in a different clause of this information sheet.

CIVIL PENALTY FOR FAILURE TO PROVIDE THE REQUIRED NOTICES
An employer that fails to provide either of the notices described above is subject to a civil penalty of $2,000 up to $5,000 for a first violation, and $5,000 up to $10,000 for each subsequent violation, recoverable by the Labor Commissioner. No penalty applies, however, where the employer's failure to notify an employee occurs at the express and specific direction or request of the federal government. For purposes of this section, an employee's "authorized representative" means an exclusive collective bargaining representative, and the section applies to both public and private employers. Nothing in the chapter containing this section restricts or limits an employer's compliance with a memorandum of understanding governing the employer's use of the federal E-Verify system.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "An employer who fails to provide the notices required by this section shall be subject to a civil penalty of two thousand dollars ($2,000) up to five thousand dollars ($5,000) for a first violation and five thousand dollars ($5,000) up to ten thousand dollars ($10,000) for each subsequent violation. This section does not require a penalty to be imposed upon an employer or person who fails to provide notice to an employee at the express and specific direction or request of the federal government. The penalty shall be recoverable by the Labor Commissioner."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 90.2(c) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Labor Code, civil penalty for failing to provide a required notice (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=90.2.)
  "an “employee’s authorized representative” means an exclusive collective bargaining representative."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 90.2(d) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Labor Code, "employee's authorized representative" defined (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=90.2.)
  "This section applies to public and private employers."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 90.2(e) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Labor Code, applies to public and private employers (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=90.2.)
  "nothing in this chapter shall be interpreted, construed, or applied to restrict or limit an employer’s compliance with a memorandum of understanding governing the use of the federal E-Verify system."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 90.2(f) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Labor Code, E-Verify memorandum of understanding savings clause (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=90.2.)
  Known gap: This is California law, used as evidence of the civil-penalty amounts, the federal-direction exception, and two definitional/scope provisions Labor Code § 90.2 attaches to the notice duties described in the two preceding clauses — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim about any specific employer's actual liability. The four citations below are all subdivisions of the same statutory section, § 90.2: (c) the penalty and federal-direction exception, (d) the "authorized representative" definition, (e) the public/private scope statement, and (f) the E-Verify savings clause. This clause does not identify who besides the Labor Commissioner, if anyone, may enforce the penalty, and does not address whether a private right of action exists — the statutory text quoted here names only the Labor Commissioner as recovering the penalty. This clause does not cover the separate, differently structured civil penalties Government Code §§ 7285.1 and 7285.2 attach to the nonpublic-area and employee-records access restrictions, addressed in separate clauses of this information sheet.

RESTRICTION ON VOLUNTARY ACCESS TO NONPUBLIC WORK AREAS
Separately from the notice duties above, California law makes it unlawful — except as otherwise required by federal law — for an employer, or a person acting on the employer's behalf, to provide voluntary consent to a federal immigration enforcement agent to enter a nonpublic area of a place of labor. This restriction does not apply if the immigration enforcement agent provides a judicial warrant. It also does not prevent an employer, or someone acting on the employer's behalf, from taking the agent to a nonpublic area where employees are not present solely to verify whether the agent has a judicial warrant, provided the employer gives no consent to search a nonpublic area in the process. An employer who violates this restriction is subject to a civil penalty of $2,000 up to $5,000 for a first violation and $5,000 up to $10,000 for each subsequent violation, except that no penalty applies if a court finds the agent was permitted to enter without the consent of the employer or other person in control of the place of labor. The restriction applies to both public and private employers, and only the Labor Commissioner or the Attorney General may enforce it, through a civil action, with any penalty recovered deposited into the Labor Enforcement and Compliance Fund.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "an employer, or a person acting on behalf of the employer, shall not provide voluntary consent to an immigration enforcement agent to enter any nonpublic areas of a place of labor. This section does not apply if the immigration enforcement agent provides a judicial warrant."
  — Cal. Gov't Code § 7285.1(a) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Government Code, bar on voluntary consent to enter a nonpublic work area (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=7285.1.)
  "An employer who violates subdivision (a) shall be subject to a civil penalty of two thousand dollars ($2,000) up to five thousand dollars ($5,000) for a first violation and five thousand dollars ($5,000) up to ten thousand dollars ($10,000) for each subsequent violation. If a court finds that an immigration enforcement agent was permitted to enter a nonpublic area of a place of labor without the consent of the employer or other person in control of the place of labor, the civil penalty shall not apply."
  — Cal. Gov't Code § 7285.1(b) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Government Code, civil penalty for an unlawful entry (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=7285.1.)
  "This section shall not preclude an employer or person acting on behalf of an employer from taking the immigration enforcement agent to a nonpublic area, where employees are not present, for the purpose of verifying whether the immigration enforcement agent has a judicial warrant, provided no consent to search nonpublic areas is given in the process."
  — Cal. Gov't Code § 7285.1(c) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Government Code, warrant-verification carve-out (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=7285.1.)
  "The exclusive authority to enforce this section is granted to the Labor Commissioner or the Attorney General and enforcement shall be through civil action. Any penalty recovered shall be deposited in the Labor Enforcement and Compliance Fund."
  — Cal. Gov't Code § 7285.1(d) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Government Code, exclusive enforcement authority (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=7285.1.)
  "This section applies to public and private employers."
  — Cal. Gov't Code § 7285.1(e) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Government Code, applies to public and private employers (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=7285.1.)
  Known gap: This is California law, used as evidence of the specific consent-to-enter restriction Government Code § 7285.1 creates and of the penalty and enforcement mechanism attached to it — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim about whether voluntary consent was or was not given in any particular encounter with a federal agent. The five citations below are subdivisions of the same statutory section, § 7285.1: (a) the consent bar and its judicial-warrant exception, (b) the penalty amounts and the no-penalty-if-a-court-finds-permission-was-given proviso, (c) the warrant-verification carve-out, (d) the exclusive-enforcement-authority and penalty-deposit provisions, and (e) the public/private scope statement. This clause does not cover Government Code § 7285.2's separate restriction on access to employee records, addressed in a different clause of this information sheet, or Government Code § 7285.3's E-Verify savings clause, whose substance duplicates Labor Code § 90.2(f) quoted in a separate clause of this information sheet. This clause also takes no position on what counts as a "public" versus "nonpublic" area of a particular workplace — a fact-specific determination the statutory text quoted here does not itself define.

RESTRICTION ON VOLUNTARY ACCESS TO EMPLOYEE RECORDS
California law also makes it unlawful — except as otherwise required by federal law — for an employer, or a person acting on the employer's behalf, to provide voluntary consent to a federal immigration enforcement agent to access, review, or obtain the employer's employee records without a subpoena or a judicial warrant. This restriction does not prohibit an employer, or someone acting on the employer's behalf, from challenging the validity of a subpoena or judicial warrant in federal district court. The restriction does not apply, however, to Form I-9 or other documents for which the employer has received a Notice of Inspection. An employer who violates this restriction is subject to a civil penalty of $2,000 up to $5,000 for a first violation and $5,000 up to $10,000 for each subsequent violation. The restriction applies to both public and private employers, and only the Labor Commissioner or the Attorney General may enforce it, through a civil action, with any penalty recovered deposited into the Labor Enforcement and Compliance Fund.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "an employer, or a person acting on behalf of the employer, shall not provide voluntary consent to an immigration enforcement agent to access, review, or obtain the employer’s employee records without a subpoena or judicial warrant. This section does not prohibit an employer, or person acting on behalf of an employer, from challenging the validity of a subpoena or judicial warrant in a federal district court."
  — Cal. Gov't Code § 7285.2(a)(1) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Government Code, bar on voluntary consent to access employee records (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=7285.2.)
  "This subdivision shall not apply to I-9 Employment Eligibility Verification forms and other documents for which a Notice of Inspection has been provided to the employer."
  — Cal. Gov't Code § 7285.2(a)(2) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Government Code, Notice-of-Inspection exception (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=7285.2.)
  "An employer who violates subdivision (a) shall be subject to a civil penalty of two thousand dollars ($2,000) up to five thousand dollars ($5,000) for a first violation and five thousand dollars ($5,000) up to ten thousand dollars ($10,000) for each subsequent violation."
  — Cal. Gov't Code § 7285.2(b) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Government Code, civil penalty for an unlawful records disclosure (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=7285.2.)
  "The exclusive authority to enforce this section is granted to the Labor Commissioner or the Attorney General and enforcement shall be through civil action. Any penalty recovered shall be deposited in the Labor Enforcement and Compliance Fund."
  — Cal. Gov't Code § 7285.2(c) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Government Code, exclusive enforcement authority (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=7285.2.)
  "This section applies to public and private employers."
  — Cal. Gov't Code § 7285.2(d) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Government Code, applies to public and private employers (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=7285.2.)
  Known gap: This is California law, used as evidence of the specific consent-to-access-records restriction Government Code § 7285.2 creates, its Notice-of-Inspection exception, and the penalty and enforcement mechanism attached to it — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim about whether voluntary consent was or was not given as to any particular record. The five citations below are subdivisions of the same statutory section, § 7285.2: (a)(1) the consent bar and the right to challenge a subpoena or warrant in federal court, (a)(2) the Notice-of-Inspection exception, (b) the penalty amounts, (c) the exclusive-enforcement-authority and penalty-deposit provisions, and (d) the public/private scope statement. This clause does not independently define "employee record" beyond the Form I-9 example the statute itself carves out from the restriction, and unlike the parallel penalty provision in Government Code § 7285.1(b), the text of § 7285.2(b) quoted here does not itself state a court-finding-based exception to the penalty — this clause draws no further conclusion from that difference in wording between the two sections. This clause does not cover Government Code § 7285.1's separate restriction on entering nonpublic work areas, addressed in a different clause of this information sheet.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
By signing below, the undersigned acknowledge that this information sheet was provided and that it states general rules of California law about an employer's notice duties and access restrictions during a federal immigration enforcement action at the workplace, rather than advice about Jane Doe's specific situation or Acme Corp.'s specific legal obligations.

expectedJSON.body: Separately from the notice duties above, California law makes it unlawful — except as otherwise required by federal law — for an employer, or a person acting on the employer's behalf, to provide voluntary consent to a federal immigration enforcement agent to enter a nonpublic area of a place of labor. This restriction does not apply if the immigration enforcement agent provides a judicial warrant. It also does not prevent an employer, or someone acting on the employer's behalf, from taking the agent to a nonpublic area where employees are not present solely to verify whether the agent has a judicial warrant, provided the employer gives no consent to search a nonpublic area in the process. An employer who violates this restriction is subject to a civil penalty of $2,000 up to $5,000 for a first violation and $5,000 up to $10,000 for each subsequent violation, except that no penalty applies if a court finds the agent was permitted to enter without the consent of the employer or other person in control of the place of labor. The restriction applies to both public and private employers, and only the Labor Commissioner or the Attorney General may enforce it, through a civil action, with any penalty recovered deposited into the Labor Enforcement and Compliance Fund.
